Explain the lazy tools mechanism: when tools are installed, what happens on first invocation, shims, mise activate/exec usage, and any caveats or drawbacks mentioned (e.g., with direnv, IDEs, scripts, shims vs activation). Quote relevant details.

result.output:
Title: Shims | mise-en-place
URL: https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html
Published: 2026-11-12

Set `lazy = true` on a tool to install it the first time one of its commands runs instead of during `mise install`.

### The Lazy Tools Mechanism

- **Bootstrap shims:** "For registry tools, mise creates bootstrap shims from the registry's command list. A tool with an explicit backend, or one that is not in the registry, names its commands with `lazy_bins`."
  ```toml
  [tools]
  node = { version = "24", lazy = true }
  ```
  ```toml
  [tools]
  "github:example/acme" = { version = "1.2.3", lazy = true, lazy_bins = ["acme", "acmectl"] }
  ```
- **First invocation:** "Running one of a lazy tool's commands installs it, plus any configured tools it depends on that are missing, and then runs the command. Nothing else is installed. This works even when `not_found_auto_install` is off."
- **Shims & Activation usage:** 
  - "Tasks, `mise exec`, and `mise env` add the bootstrap shims behind the tool directories whenever the toolset has a lazy tool, so a task installs a lazy tool the first time it runs one of its commands."
  - "After installation, `mise activate` puts the real tool ahead of its shim, so later calls cost nothing extra."
  - "`mise activate --shims` keeps dispatching every call through mise."
  - "`mise use` rebuilds shims when it changes a lazy declaration; run `mise reshim` after editing one by hand."

### Caveats and Drawbacks
- **Precedence:** "A lazy declaration never overrides a higher-precedence config that selects the same tool without `lazy`."
- **Command behavior:** "`mise run` does not install lazy tools ahead of time."
- **Installation commands:** "A bare `mise install` skips lazy tools, and a bare `mise upgrade` skips the ones that are not installed yet. `mise install --include-lazy` installs them all now, and `mise install node` or `mise upgrade node` installs one. `mise outdated` still lists them, marked `[MISSING] (lazy)`."
- **Safe mode:** "In safe mode, lazy tools in project config get no bootstrap shims and do not install on first use. Neither does a lazy option that a project's `[tool_alias]` adds to a tool in global config."

content.text:
I now have enough evidence — including two reproduced failure modes. Here's my assessment.

## Verdict

Mixed: one or two of the four entries are reasonable, but **as written the diff breaks fresh-clone onboarding in two concrete, reproduced ways**. The `go` entry is the most harmful.

## What the change does

`lazy = true` defers installation from `mise install` to the first invocation of one of the tool's commands, via "bootstrap shims" (per the [shims docs](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html#lazy-tools)): a bare `mise install` skips lazy tools entirely; `mise install --include-lazy` forces them. The repo already uses this pattern for `copilot`, so the diff extends an existing precedent to `go`, `node`, `vendir`, and `npm:renovate`.

## Reproduced problems

### 1. `go = { version = "1.26", lazy = true }` breaks `mise install` on fresh machines

`mise install` doesn't just skip `go` — it **hard-fails**, because the *eagerly* installed `go:entireio/external-agents…entire-agent-goose` tool (not marked lazy) needs the project's `go@1.26` to build, and bare install won't install it. I reproduced this in an isolated data dir with no host Go on `PATH`:

```
✗ go:github.com/entireio/external-agents/.../entire-agent-goose … failed:
  requires configured install dependency 'go@1.26', but its selected version is not installed
mise ERROR installation failed; previous lockfiles were preserved
```

That is exactly the README onboarding path (`mise install --locked`) on a fresh clone. The lazy declaration buys nothing here: the goose agent tool is installed eagerly anyway, so `go` gets needed immediately at setup time. To make `go` workably lazy you'd also have to make the go:-backend tool lazy — but that's an explicit backend with no registry bin metadata, i.e. it hits problem 2 below and needs `lazy_bins`, and it would defer the agent runtime itself, which coding agents depend on. Simplest: revert `go` to a plain pin.

### 2. `npm:renovate` lazy is silently inert — and takes `mise run check` down with it

mise only creates bootstrap shims from *registry* bin metadata; a tool with an explicit backend (`npm:`) must declare `lazy_bins` explicitly. Without it, mise emits (reproduced):

```
mise WARN  Skipping invalid lazy shim declaration: lazy tool npm:chalk has no registry bin metadata; set lazy_bins explicitly
mise WARN  failed to create shims for lazy tools
```

The diff has no `lazy_bins`, so no bootstrap shims exist for `renovate` / `renovate-config-validator` → on a fresh clone, `renovate-config-validator` is plain *command not found* when the `hk check --all` lint gate (hk.pkl `renovate-config-validator` step) runs it — i.e. the mandated `mise run check` fails. If you keep the lazy flag, you need `lazy_bins = ["renovate", "renovate-config-validator"]`.

## Remaining drawbacks (if fixed per above)

- **Deferred, not avoided.** `renovate` is not a "rarely needed" tool here — the lint gate you run on every change needs it. Lazy just moves a multi-hundred-MB npm install (plus `node`) from `mise install` into the middle of the first `mise run check`: a slow, noisy, network-dependent first lint whose failure is less legible than a setup-time error. Onboarding gets *faster setup but worse first experience*.
- **Weakened setup guarantee.** After `mise install --locked` succeeds, "everything pinned is present" no longer holds. Related open question worth verifying: the Renovate desync check documented in `.github/renovate.json` relies on `mise install --locked` erroring when `mise.toml`/`mise.lock` disagree — if bare install skips lazy tools without resolving them, that check may no longer validate the lazy entries' pins.
- **CI.** The `skills-update` workflow runs `vendir sync` directly after `mise-action` (which does a bare `mise install`). With lazy `vendir` this works via the bootstrap shim (registry metadata exists for it), but the install now happens inside a cron step — a transient network blip fails the weekly sync at point-of-use instead of failing visibly at setup.
- **Coding agents.** In mise-activated shells agents get the bootstrap shims, so first use auto-installs — but that means a mid-task multi-minute install with progress noise, and any agent/env *without* mise activation (PATH-stripped shells, bare CI, `docker exec` without mise env) gets a bare "command not found" that's harder to diagnose than a missing tool after a failed install. (This very session is unaffected — all four tools are already installed locally.)

## What's actually fine

- `vendir` is the good case: used only by the weekly skills sync, registry tool (bootstrap shim works), genuinely deferrable.
- `node` in principle: nothing else in the repo consumes node eagerly, and a properly-`lazy_bins`-fixed `npm:renovate` would pull `node` along on first use. It's coherent as a pair with renovate.

So without `--include-lazy`, every cache miss re-installs the deferred tool mid-step, each run. With `--include-lazy`, the tools land during the cached install step. ## Content

# Change and release workflow

## Before starting

- Check the current branch first (`git status`): **Always work on a branch named `agent-<topic>`**, create one if needed
  (based off of `main`, i.e. `git switch -c agent-<topic> main`).
- If work belongs on a branch but a stray commit already landed on `main`: move it
  (`git switch -c agent-…; git branch -f main <upstream-tip>`) and disclose it to the user.
- Never stage unrelated WIP: check `git status` before staging and add files explicitly.

## Commits

- Conventional Commits (`build`, `chore:`, `ci`, `docs:`, `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style`,
  `test`); scope app changes (`fix(nfs-server): …`); one commit per logical unit.
- Final trailer line: `Assisted-by: Goose:<model-slug>` – the model name without provider prefix, e.g.
  `Assisted-by: Goose:glm-5.3-flash`.
- The commit-msg hook enforces the format; escape hatch `HK=0 git commit`.

## Before finishing a change

Run `mise run check` – lint plus validate; it is the same gate CI runs. Lint-stack details and scoped checking: skill
`ha-app-tooling`. Task usage: `mise run check --help`.

## App releases

- A working branch starting from `main` bumps `version` in `config.yaml` to a **single** next version (major, minor or
  patch by semantic versioning): the branch ships one version, not one per commit, and continuously expands that
  version's `CHANGELOG.md` entry until it lands on `main`.
- Transitory extra versions within the branch are fine where testing demands one (AppArmor profile changes are only
  re-applied on app *update*, never on rebuild) – squash them back into the single version (config plus one merged
  changelog entry) before merging.
- CI enforces the rule: `.github/workflows/version-guard.yaml` fails when device-visible app files (`rootfs/`,
  `Dockerfile`, `config.yaml`, `apparmor.txt`, `translations/`) changed without a version bump – the Supervisor's update
  model makes a no-bump change a silent no-op that only repoints an already-published version tag. Exception: if the
  base version's GHCR tag was never published (its release's build/publish failed), the guard probes GHCR and passes –
  reusing the version then repoints nothing; unprovable fails closed. Changes to docs-only files (README, DOCS,
  CHANGELOG, KNOWLEDGE, TODO, `.agents/`), the per-app `.dockerignore` (it shapes the build context but never changes
  the image the device receives), and repo tooling do not require a version bump.

## CI/CD is the source of truth for what gets published

- Pushes to `main` build and publish images (`.github/workflows/builder.yaml`). If CI fails, fix the repo, not CI config
  – unless the CI config itself is wrong.
- Builder caveats: the init job needs `fetch-depth: 0` – the changed-files filter otherwise only sees the tip commit and
  silently skips multi-commit merges, so use regular merges instead of squash merges.
- The app `Dockerfile` must not pull from Docker Hub at build time (rule and rationale: skill `ha-app-scaffolding`).
- The lint workflow runs frenck's app linter natively (pinned source plus pypi requirements), not via its Docker action
  (whose Docker Hub image builds flaked with 504s and 429 runner-pool rate limits).
- In `.github/workflows/`, match GitHub users and bots by immutable user id, never by `login` (root `KNOWLEDGE.md`
  §"GitHub Actions: user identity matching").

## Device access

Testing against the real HA device over SSH only on explicit user request; otherwise hand the user exact commands to
run. On-device procedures: skill `ha-app-device-testing`.

## Version-sensitive facts

Supervisor schemas, s6-overlay layout, HAOS kernel configs and HA docs change frequently. Wherever such facts are
written down (`KNOWLEDGE.md`, comments, skills), cite the source (URL plus version/ref). Before relying on them for new
work, re-verify against the latest docs/source.

## Design change proposals

When a fix reveals a design issue, diagnose hands-on first (strace, packet captures, a reproduction lab), then explain
root cause, options and trade-offs to the user before rewriting.

## Text files

Every text file ends with a final newline (the lint gate enforces it).

Done. Summary:

- **Branch**: `agent-mise-lazy-install`, based on `agent-renovate-automerge`'s tip rather than `main` — the copilot-consuming `action-bump-review.yaml` only exists on that branch, so branching off `main` would have had no target file.

  - `.github/workflows/skills-update.yaml` (consumes `vendir sync`)
  - `.github/workflows/action-bump-review.yaml` (consumes `copilot`)
- **Verification**: scoped `hk check` on the two files — all steps green (jactionlint, ryl lint/format, zizmor, final-newline). I did not run the full `mise run check` gate since the change touches only these two files; CI will run the full gate on push.

One live confirmation from this run: while the commit hook executed, mise emitted against your working-tree `mise.toml`:

```
mise WARN  Skipping invalid lazy shim declaration: lazy tool npm:renovate has no registry bin metadata; set lazy_bins explicitly
```

— which independently corroborates the earlier finding that `npm:renovate = { …, lazy = true }` as written produces no bootstrap shims and would leave `renovate-config-validator` unresolvable on fresh clones.
